title: Formal Verification Test Log

canonical_node.axiom: Formal verification preserves the actual path of testing, including mistakes and boundary discoveries, and does not overclaim what is proven.
definitions: LawIso: a minimal isomorphism structure with zero/one value function, collapsed predicate, bidirectional map, value preservation, and collapse preservation.
RichLawIso: an enriched isomorphism structure adding regime-role preservation and forward/reverse transition preservation.
Bridge matrix: an encoding of ten formal factor slots (G M E S T K R Q F C) with physical and spiritual readings and product behavior.
Proof escape hatch: any use of sorry, admit, axiom, or unsafe in the Lean module path.
derivation: The minimal LawIso definition admits any binary zero/one system with the same collapse pattern, as shown by the coin false positive.
Adding regime roles and transition preservation to RichLawIso blocks the natural coin model but still admits a relabeled coin with the same roles.
The bridge matrix rejects semantic swaps when encoded signatures differ, but cannot verify the domain-faithfulness of assigned signatures.
Therefore, formal verification establishes preservation of encoded structure, not the truth of the domain interpretation.
canonical_node.action: Preserve the actual verification path, including adversarial tests and boundary discoveries, and clearly distinguish verified claims from not-yet-supported claims.
boundary: Does not claim that Lean verifies domain interpretations or the correctness of human-assigned semantic roles.
Does not claim that the encoded signatures are domain-faithful without an external source-grounding layer.
Does not claim that the absence of proof escape hatches in the active module path guarantees the absence of all possible flaws.
test: Run lake build and lake env lean IsomorphismTest.lean.
Scan the active Lean module path for sorry, admit, axiom, and unsafe.
Run adversarial tests such as coin false positives and semantic swaps to expose specification boundaries.
Check that corrected claims explicitly separate verified formal results from domain-interpretation claims.

dg1_dependencies: Lean theorem prover and project build environment
dg_protocol.dg2_new_capability: Provides a disciplined method for recording formal verification attempts, adversarial tests, and boundary discoveries, preventing overclaiming of formal results.
dg_protocol.dg3_preserved_floor: Preserves the distinction between verified formal claims and domain-interpretation claims, and records the actual path of testing including mistakes.
dg_protocol.dg4_collapse_if_removed: Without this log, the project would lose the record of boundary discoveries and corrected claims, risking overclaiming of what Lean proves.
dg5_translation_registers: RichLawIso -> enriched abstraction test with roles and transitions
Bridge matrix -> internal consistency test of encoded signatures

classification.recommended_atom_action: preserve as a methodological guardrail for formal verification practice

overstatement_risks: Claiming that Lean verifies domain interpretations when it only verifies preservation of encoded structure.
Claiming that the absence of proof escape hatches guarantees full correctness.
Claiming that the bridge matrix is domain-faithful without external source grounding.
kill_conditions: If the log is used to claim that Lean has verified the strong-force/love bridge in a domain-rich sense.
If the log is used to claim that the encoded signatures are the correct scientific or theological interpretations.
risk.lean_target: Formal verification of encoded structure preservation, not domain truth.

plain_summary: This document is a test log for Lean formal verification of theological-physical bridges. It records positive results, adversarial tests, and boundary discoveries, emphasizing that Lean verifies preservation of encoded structure but cannot verify the correctness of human-assigned semantic roles. The log includes minimal and enriched isomorphism tests, a bridge matrix, and explicit corrected claims. It serves as a methodological guardrail against overclaiming formal results.
